stimuli.text: Initial-rate data for A + B → products:
A student heats 2.3 g of $$\ce{CaCO3(s)}$$, which decomposes completely: $$\ce{CaCO3(s) -> CaO(s) + CO2(g)}$$. The $$\ce{CO2}$$ is collected at 306 K and 1.04 atm.
The decomposition of compound X was monitored at constant temperature.
A student titrates 29.0 mL of 0.17 M weak monoprotic acid HA (Ka = 1.8 \times 10^{-5}) with 0.17 M NaOH.
4.7 g of $$\ce{NH4NO3}$$ dissolves in 138 g of water in a coffee-cup calorimeter. The temperature falls by 6.2 °C. Assume the solution's specific heat is 4.18 J/(g·°C).

A galvanic cell is made of a Ni electrode in 1.0 M $$\ce{Ni^{2+}}$$ and a Pb electrode in 1.0 M $$\ce{Pb^{2+}}$$. Standard reduction potentials: $$\ce{Ni^{2+} + 2e- -> Ni}$$ E° = -0.25 V; $$\ce{Pb^{2+} + 2e- -> Pb}$$ E° = -0.13 V.
The photoelectron spectra of N (Z = 7) and O (Z = 8) are compared.

questions.stem: What is the pH of a 0.1 M solution of $$\ce{HNO3}$$ at 25 °C?

options.why: Correct. Strong acid: [H₃O⁺] equals its concentration.
Strong acids and bases ionize completely; no equilibrium is needed.

questions.stem: What is the pH of a 0.001 M solution of $$\ce{HCl}$$ at 25 °C?

options.why: Correct. Strong acid: [H₃O⁺] equals its concentration.
Strong acids and bases ionize completely; no equilibrium is needed.

questions.stem: What is the molarity of a solution made by dissolving 0.195 mol of solute in enough water to make 693 mL of solution?
A reaction has a theoretical yield of 17 g. The actual yield is 14.4 g. What is the percent yield?
Why is HI a stronger acid than HF?

options.text: F is less electronegative than I
The H–I bond is weaker and I⁻ is larger, so H⁺ is released more easily
options.why: Correct. Bond strength decreases down the group.

questions.explanation: Bond strength decreases down the group.

questions.stem: Is $$\ce{PCl3}$$ polar or nonpolar, and why?

options.text: Nonpolar, because its bond dipoles cancel by symmetry
options.why: Consider the molecule's shape, not only its bonds.

options.text: Nonpolar, because it has no polar bonds
options.why: Polarity depends on both bond polarity and geometry.

options.text: Polar, because its bond dipoles do not cancel

options.why: Containing H does not make a molecule polar.

questions.explanation: PCl3 is trigonal pyramidal; the dipoles do not cancel.

questions.stem: A solution has an absorbance of 1.72 in a 2 cm cuvette. The molar absorptivity is 287 M⁻¹cm⁻¹. What is the concentration?
Why does temperature remain constant while ice melts?

options.text: Added energy overcomes intermolecular forces rather than increasing kinetic energy
options.why: Correct. Phase changes occur at constant temperature.

options.text: Covalent bonds in water are breaking
options.why: Melting does not break covalent bonds.

questions.explanation: Phase changes occur at constant temperature.

questions.stem: A first-order reaction has a half-life of 28 min. Starting at 11 M, what is the concentration after 84 min?

options.why: Each half-life halves the concentration; it is not divided by 2n.

questions.stem: What is the mass percent of H in $$\ce{C2H5OH}$$?

options.why: Use masses, not numbers of atoms.
There are 6 atoms of H in the formula.
That is the percent of the other elements.

questions.stem: Samples of $$\ce{H2}$$, $$\ce{O2}$$, $$\ce{Ar}$$, $$\ce{CH4}$$ are all at the same temperature. Which has the highest average molecular speed?

options.why: CH4 has a larger molar mass (16 g/mol).
O2 has a larger molar mass (32 g/mol).
Correct. At the same temperature, average kinetic energy is equal, so the lightest gas moves fastest.
Ar has a larger molar mass (40 g/mol).

questions.explanation: Molar masses: H2 2.02, O2 32, Ar 40, CH4 16.

questions.stem: Which bond is the most polar?

options.why: Correct. It has the largest electronegativity difference (1.8).

questions.stem: A gas mixture contains 0.9 mol N₂, 0.7 mol O₂ and 0.8 mol Ar at a total pressure of 4.1 atm. What is the partial pressure of N₂?

options.why: The gases are not present in equal amounts.
Use the mole fraction, not moles.

questions.stem: Which is the strongest acid?

options.why: Correct. More oxygen atoms stabilize the conjugate base.

questions.explanation: More oxygen atoms stabilize the conjugate base.

questions.stem: For $$\ce{A(g) + B(g) <=> 2C(g)}$$, K = 7.6. A mixture has [A] = 0.5 M, [B] = 0.2 M and [C] = 0.2 M. In which direction will the reaction proceed?

options.text: It is at equilibrium, because Q = K
It proceeds forward, toward products, because Q = 0.4
options.why: Correct. Q = [C]²/([A][B]) = 0.4, which is less than K.

options.text: It proceeds in reverse, toward reactants, because Q = 0.4
options.why: If Q is less than K, the reaction proceeds forward.

options.text: It proceeds forward, toward products, because Q = 2

questions.stem: In a mechanism, a species that is produced in one step and consumed in a later step is a(n):

options.why: Correct. It does not appear in the overall equation.
A catalyst is consumed first and regenerated later.

questions.explanation: It does not appear in the overall equation.

questions.stem: On a reaction energy profile, the reactants are at 109 kJ/mol, the transition state at 188 kJ/mol and the products at 31 kJ/mol. What is ΔH for the reaction?

options.why: Measure from the correct starting point.

questions.explanation: Forward Ea = 79, ΔH = -78, reverse Ea = 157 kJ/mol.

questions.stem: Which is the ground-state electron configuration of potassium (K, Z = 19)?

options.why: Correct. Fill orbitals in order until 19 electrons are placed.

questions.stem: How can an unfavorable reaction (ΔG positive) be made to occur?

options.text: By coupling it to a favorable reaction so the total ΔG is negative

questions.stem: 96 mL of 3.6 M solution is diluted to 330 mL. What is the new concentration?

options.why: V₂ is the total final volume.

questions.stem: What is the pressure of 0.24 mol of gas in a 18 L container at 337 K?

options.why: With L and atm, use R = 0.08206.

questions.stem: For the elementary step 2NO + Cl₂ → 2NOCl, what is the rate law?

options.text: It cannot be determined without experiment

options.why: Correct. Elementary steps use their coefficients as exponents.

questions.explanation: Elementary steps use their coefficients as exponents.

questions.stem: A weak acid HA has pKa = 8.2. In a solution at pH 7.3, which statement is correct?

options.why: Correct. Below the pKa, the protonated form dominates.

questions.stem: A 48.6 mL sample of $$\ce{H2SO4}$$ is titrated to the equivalence point with 28.1 mL of 0.192 M NaOH. What is the concentration of the acid?

options.why: Correct. Each H₂SO₄ reacts with two OH⁻, so divide the moles of NaOH by 2.

questions.stem: What is the energy of a photon with a wavelength of 727 nm?

options.why: Correct. E = hc/λ, with λ in meters.

questions.stem: A mass spectrum of a sample of lithium shows two peaks: mass 6 with relative abundance 40% and mass 7 with 60%. What is the average atomic mass of the sample?

options.why: Pair each mass with its own abundance.
The isotopes are not equally abundant.
Correct. Weight each isotope mass by its fractional abundance.

questions.stem: What is the energy of a photon with a wavelength of 389 nm?

options.why: Correct. E = hc/λ, with λ in meters.

questions.stem: What is the oxidation number of Mn in $$\ce{MnO4^-}$$?

options.why: Correct. The oxidation numbers must sum to the species' overall charge (O usually −2, H usually +1).
Make the oxidation numbers add up to the overall charge.
Make the oxidation numbers add up to the overall charge.
Make the oxidation numbers add up to the overall charge.

questions.stem: A gas mixture contains 0.2 mol N₂, 0.7 mol O₂ and 0.9 mol Ar at a total pressure of 2.9 atm. What is the partial pressure of N₂?

options.why: Use the mole fraction, not moles.
The gases are not present in equal amounts.

questions.stem: Adding an inert gas to a reaction mixture at constant volume does what to the equilibrium?

options.text: Nothing; partial pressures of the reacting gases are unchanged
Shifts it toward more gas moles
Shifts it toward fewer gas moles

questions.stem: How many moles are in 6 g of $$\ce{C3H8}$$?

options.why: Correct. n = m/M with M = 44.09 g/mol.

questions.stem: The Ksp of $$\ce{Mg(OH)2}$$ is 5.6 \times 10^{-12}. What is its molar solubility in pure water?
Reaction 1 has ΔH₁ = -419 kJ and reaction 2 has ΔH₂ = -246 kJ. A target reaction is obtained by doubling reaction 1 and reversing reaction 2. What is ΔH for the target reaction?

options.why: Enthalpies add; they do not multiply.
Correct. Reverse → change sign; multiply → multiply ΔH; then add.
Reversing changes the sign of ΔH₂.

questions.stem: For $$\ce{A(g) + B(g) <=> 2C(g)}$$, K = 5.5. A mixture has [A] = 0.3 M, [B] = 0.6 M and [C] = 0.9 M. In which direction will the reaction proceed?

options.text: It proceeds in reverse, toward reactants, because Q = 4.5
options.why: If Q is less than K, the reaction proceeds forward.

options.text: It proceeds forward, toward products, because Q = 4.5
options.why: Correct. Q = [C]²/([A][B]) = 4.5, which is less than K.

options.text: It is at equilibrium, because Q = K
It proceeds forward, toward products, because Q = 5

questions.stem: Which formula is most likely for the compound of element X (Group 2) and element Y (Group 16)?
How many valence electrons are shown in the Lewis structure of $$\ce{CH4}$$?

options.why: Correct. Sum the valence electrons of all atoms, then add one per negative charge (subtract one per positive charge).

questions.stem: A reaction has K = 29. What is K for the reaction multiplied by ½?

options.why: Correct. Reverse → 1/K; multiply by n → Kⁿ.
K is raised to a power, not multiplied.
Multiplying by n raises K to the nth power.

questions.stem: Which compound has the greater lattice energy, $$\ce{BaO}$$ or $$\ce{NaCl}$$?

options.text: $$\ce{NaCl}$$, because its ions have larger charges
They are equal because both are ionic
$$\ce{NaCl}$$, because it has more atoms per formula unit
options.why: Number of atoms does not determine lattice energy.

options.text: $$\ce{BaO}$$, because its ions have larger charges
options.why: Correct. By Coulomb's law, attraction increases with the product of the ion charges.

questions.explanation: BaO has ion charges 2 and 2; NaCl has 1 and 1.

questions.stem: Under which conditions does a real gas deviate most from ideal behavior?

options.why: Correct. Particle volume and attractions matter most.

questions.explanation: Particle volume and attractions matter most.

questions.stem: Which Lewis structure is preferred when formal charges are considered?

options.text: The one with the largest formal charges
The one with formal charges closest to zero and any negative charge on the most electronegative atom
options.why: Correct. That is the formal charge criterion.

options.text: The one with positive charge on the most electronegative atom
The one with the most double bonds

questions.explanation: That is the formal charge criterion.

questions.stem: 63 g of water at 55 °C is mixed with 51 g of water at 23 °C in an insulated container. What is the final temperature?

options.why: Pair each mass with its own temperature.
Correct. Heat lost = heat gained; for water alone, a mass-weighted average.

questions.stem: What is the molarity of a solution made by dissolving 0.192 mol of solute in enough water to make 584 mL of solution?
For $$\ce{4NH3 + 5O2 -> 4NO + 6H2O}$$, $$\ce{O2}$$ is consumed at 0.58 M/s. At what rate does $$\ce{H2O}$$ form?

options.why: Divide by the reactant's coefficient too.
Correct. Multiply by the coefficient ratio 6/5.

questions.stem: Use the bond enthalpies to estimate ΔH for $$\ce{N2 + 3H2 -> 2NH3}$$.

options.why: Broken minus formed, not formed minus broken.
Bonds formed release energy: subtract them.
Multiply each bond energy by the number of bonds.
Correct. ΔH ≈ Σ(bonds broken) − Σ(bonds formed).

questions.stem: What is the molarity of a solution made by dissolving 0.061 mol of solute in enough water to make 175 mL of solution?
For $$\ce{2H2 + O2 -> 2H2O}$$, 45 g of $$\ce{H2}$$ reacts with 53 g of $$\ce{O2}$$. What mass of $$\ce{H2O}$$ can form?

options.why: Not all of both reactants reacts.
Use the limiting reactant, which gives less product.
Correct. O2 is the limiting reactant.
Apply the mole ratio from the equation.

questions.stem: For $$\ce{H2(g) + I2(g) <=> 2HI(g)}$$, initial [H₂] = 0.9 M and [I₂] = 1.3 M, with no HI. At equilibrium, [HI] = 0.84 M. What is K?
For $$\ce{2Na + Cl2 -> 2NaCl}$$, 35 g of $$\ce{Na}$$ reacts with 74 g of $$\ce{Cl2}$$. What mass of $$\ce{NaCl}$$ can form?

options.why: Not all of both reactants reacts.
Correct. Na is the limiting reactant.
Apply the mole ratio from the equation.
Use the limiting reactant, which gives less product.

questions.stem: For the galvanic cell made from these half-cells, what is ΔG°? (F = 96,485 C/mol)

options.why: ΔG° is negative for a positive E°.
Correct. ΔG° = −nFE° with n = 6 electrons transferred and E° = 1.41 V.

questions.stem: Calculate ΔH° for $$\ce{2C2H6 + 7O2 -> 4CO2 + 6H2O(g)}$$. (ΔH°f of O₂ is 0.)

options.why: Correct. Σ n ΔH°f(products) − Σ n ΔH°f(reactants).
Multiply each ΔH°f by its coefficient.

questions.stem: At 298 K, ΔG° for a reaction is -15 kJ/mol. What is K?

options.why: Correct. K = e^(−ΔG°/RT), with ΔG° in J/mol and R = 8.314.

questions.explanation: ln K = 6.05; K = 426. Negative ΔG°: K greater than 1.

questions.stem: How should acetic acid be written in a net ionic equation?

options.why: Correct. It is a weak acid and mostly un-ionized.

options.text: It is always omitted as a spectator

questions.explanation: It is a weak acid and mostly un-ionized.

questions.stem: When a reaction involving 0.014 mol of limiting reactant occurs in 113 g of solution (c = 4.18 J/(g·°C)), the temperature rises by 12.4 °C. What is ΔH for the reaction?

options.why: Divide by the moles of reactant.
A temperature rise means the reaction is exothermic (negative ΔH).
Correct. q(solution) = mcΔT = 5860 J; q(reaction) = −q(solution); divide by moles.

questions.stem: A reaction has ΔH° = 140 kJ/mol and ΔS° = 175 J/(mol·K). Above what temperature is it thermodynamically favorable?

options.why: Correct. Set ΔG = 0: T = ΔH/ΔS (with ΔH in J).
Convert ΔH to J (or ΔS to kJ).

questions.stem: A weak acid (pKa 6.35) is titrated with NaOH; the equivalence point is reached at 27.9 mL. What is the pH after 13.9 mL of NaOH has been added?

options.why: Correct. At the half-equivalence point, [HA] = [A⁻], so pH = pKa.
That is only for strong acid–strong base equivalence.

questions.stem: What is the pH of a 1 M solution of nitrous acid (Ka = 4.5 \times 10^{-4})?

options.why: A weak acid does not ionize completely.
Correct. Solve Ka = x²/(C − x) for x = [H₃O⁺].

questions.stem: A galvanic cell is built from Al/$$\ce{Al^{3+}}$$ and Ag/$$\ce{Ag+}$$ half-cells. Which electrode is the anode?

options.text: Ag, where reduction occurs at the anode
options.why: Reduction occurs at the cathode, not the anode.
The higher potential is reduced at the cathode.
Correct. The half-reaction with the lower reduction potential runs as oxidation at the anode.

questions.explanation: Al (E° -1.66 V) is oxidized at the anode; Ag is reduced at the cathode.

questions.stem: A compound (hydrogen peroxide) is 5.93% H, 94.1% O by mass. What is its empirical formula?

options.why: That is the molecular formula; reduce to the simplest ratio.
Correct. Convert each percent (in 100 g) to moles and divide by the smallest.

questions.explanation: The mole ratio reduces to HO; the molecular formula is H2O2.

questions.stem: A buffer contains 0.23 mol of a weak acid HA (pKa 9.25) and 0.35 mol of A⁻. What is its pH?
What is the rate law?

options.why: Compare trials where only one concentration changes.
Recheck how the rate changes when [B] doubles.
Orders are found from the data, not from coefficients.
Correct. Doubling [A] multiplies the rate by 4; doubling [B] multiplies it by 2.

questions.explanation: Trials 1→2: rate ×4, so order 2 in A. Trials 1→3: rate ×2, so order 1 in B.

parts.prompt: Calculate the number of moles of CO₂ produced.

rubric.criterion: Correct moles using molar mass 100.09 g/mol and the 1:1 ratio.

parts.prompt: Calculate the volume of CO₂ expected.
The student measures 0.494 L of gas. Calculate the percent yield, and give one experimental reason the yield could be less than 100%.

rubric.example: Incomplete decomposition (not heated long enough) or gas leaking from the apparatus.

parts.prompt: Draw (describe) a complete Lewis diagram for CO₂, and identify its molecular geometry and the hybridization of carbon.

rubric.example: O=C=O with two lone pairs on each O (16 valence electrons).

parts.prompt: Explain why CO₂ is nonpolar even though C=O bonds are polar.

rubric.criterion: Linear symmetry makes the bond dipoles cancel.

parts.prompt: CaO is an ionic solid. Explain, using Coulomb's law, why CaO has a higher melting point than KCl.

rubric.criterion: Larger ion charges in CaO (2+/2−) than in KCl (1+/1−).
Greater electrostatic attraction (and smaller ions) means more energy is needed to separate the ions.

parts.prompt: Calculate the average rate of disappearance of X between 0 and 20 s.
Determine the order of the reaction with respect to X. Justify your answer using the data.

rubric.example: Equal time intervals give equal changes in 1/[X].

parts.prompt: Write the rate law and determine the rate constant, with units.
Calculate the half-life of the reaction (for the initial concentration).
A proposed mechanism has a slow first step: 2X → X₂. Is the mechanism consistent with the rate law? Explain.

rubric.criterion: Yes; the slow step's elementary rate law matches the observed rate law.

parts.prompt: A catalyst is added. Explain its effect on the rate and on the rate constant, using activation energy.

rubric.example: The catalyst provides a new pathway.

rubric.criterion: Lower activation energy means a larger fraction of collisions are successful.

parts.prompt: Write the net ionic equation for the titration reaction.
Calculate the initial pH of the acid solution.

rubric.criterion: Ka expression set up with x = [H₃O⁺].

parts.prompt: Calculate the volume of NaOH needed to reach the equivalence point.
What is the pH at the half-equivalence point? Justify.
Calculate the pH at the equivalence point.

rubric.criterion: Uses Kb = Kw/Ka and the diluted [A⁻].

parts.prompt: Choose an appropriate indicator from: methyl orange (pKa 3.7), bromothymol blue (pKa 7.0), phenolphthalein (pKa 9.3). Justify.

rubric.criterion: Indicator whose pKa is closest to the equivalence pH.

parts.prompt: Explain why the solution at the half-equivalence point resists pH change when a small amount of HCl is added.

rubric.criterion: A⁻ reacts with added H⁺ to form HA (buffer).
rubric.example: A⁻ + H₃O⁺ → HA + H₂O, so the ratio [A⁻]/[HA] changes only slightly.

parts.prompt: Is the dissolution endothermic or exothermic? Justify.

rubric.example: Endothermic: the solution cooled, so energy was absorbed.

parts.prompt: Calculate the heat absorbed or released by the solution.
Calculate ΔH of dissolution in kJ/mol.
If some heat escaped to the surroundings, would the magnitude of the calculated ΔH be too large or too small? Explain.

rubric.criterion: Too small, because the measured temperature change is smaller than the true change.

parts.prompt: Write the balanced net ionic equation for the cell reaction.
Calculate E°cell.
Calculate ΔG° for the cell reaction.
The concentration of Ni²⁺ is increased to 2.0 M. Predict the effect on the cell potential and justify.

rubric.criterion: E decreases because Q increases (a product's concentration rises).
rubric.example: Q greater than 1 → E less than E°.

questions.title: Solubility of a slightly soluble salt

parts.prompt: Write the Ksp expression.
Calculate the molar solubility in pure water.
Calculate the molar solubility in a solution containing 0.1 M I⁻ (from a soluble salt).
Would lowering the pH significantly change the solubility? Explain.

rubric.criterion: Correct reasoning about whether the anion is basic.
rubric.example: No: I⁻ is the conjugate base of a strong acid, so H⁺ does not remove it.

parts.prompt: Write the electron configuration of O.
Explain why the 1s peak of O has a higher binding energy than the 1s peak of N.

rubric.criterion: O has more protons, so 1s electrons are attracted more strongly (Coulomb's law).

parts.prompt: Describe one difference in the number or relative height of peaks between the two spectra.

rubric.criterion: A valid difference based on configurations.
rubric.example: O has one more electron, so its outermost peak is taller or an extra peak appears.

parts.prompt: Which element has the larger atomic radius? Justify using Coulomb's law.

rubric.criterion: N: fewer protons with similar shielding, so valence electrons are held less tightly.
rubric.example: Same period; effective nuclear charge increases across.
